title: Hardware-aware quantum attention for fast radio burst identification
authors: Li He, Xuan Yang, Feng Xiong, Songbo Zhang, Qiuhao Chen, Yuchen He, Yunxiang Yang, Jun Lu, Claudio Furtado, Amilcar R. Queiroz, Xinping Deng, Yang Wu, Xuefeng Wu
abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration extragalactic pulses whose discovery requires searches over large signal-parameter spaces and the rejection of candidate sets dominated by radio-frequency interference and noise. Integrating quantum processors into FRB searches requires a workflow connecting telescop data to hardware-compatible models. Here we develop a pipeline that converts raw search-mode PSRFITS data into dynamic-spectrum segments and identifies FRB-like signals using a hybrid Quantum Vision Transformer (QViT). On labelled FAST data, the selected QViT achieves a mean accuracy of 94.00% and recall of 98.30%, with similar performance to a compact classical Vision Transformer. Recall reaches 97.11% on an FRB source excluded from training and model selection. Real-device execution on 82 segments yields a mean simulator-hardware Hellinger fidelity of 0.9161 +/- 0.0074. The workflow connects raw telescope data to quantum-assisted identification and provides an experimental basis for assessing the measurement requirements that must be addressed before survey-scale deployment.
summary: This paper proposes a Quantum Vision Transformer (QViT) to accelerate the identification of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) from raw telescope data. It integrates quantum processors into the data processing pipeline, achieving high classification accuracy comparable to classical methods. The work provides crucial metrics, including hardware fidelity, to assess the feasibility of deploying quantum algorithms for large-scale astrophysical surveys.
main_problem: The core problem is identifying Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) from massive amounts of raw telescope data while integrating quantum computation into the search pipeline.
main_result: The developed Quantum Vision Transformer (QViT) achieves high classification accuracy (e.g., 94.00% accuracy, 98.30% recall) and demonstrates strong hardware compatibility, with a mean simulator-hardware Hellinger fidelity of 0.9161.
method: The authors developed a hybrid quantum-classical pipeline where parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) replace the linear projection layers in a standard Vision Transformer (ViT) to generate quantum-enhanced Query, Key, and Value representations.
model_or_system: The system uses raw PSRFITS data from FAST observations, which are preprocessed into dynamic-spectrum images ($288 	imes 288$). The model is the QViT, which utilizes PQCs to encode data features into quantum states for attention mechanism calculations.
key_observables: Accuracy, Recall, F2 score, Mean simulator-hardware Hellinger fidelity (0.9161 $\pm$ 0.0074), and Mean cosine similarity (0.9853 $\pm$ 0.0022).
important_parameters: Qubit count ($n_q=6$), number of heads ($n_h=4$), and the specific architecture parameters of the PQC circuits.
main_assumptions: The study acknowledges that practical quantum benefit must account for overheads like data loading, state preparation, and measurement, and that high fidelity does not guarantee identical final classification decisions.
figures_summary: Figures compare QViT vs. ViT performance across test sets, showing high fidelity between simulated and measured quantum feature vectors, and demonstrating QViT's performance relative to ViT.
paper_structure: The paper details the data preprocessing from raw PSRFITS data into images, introduces the QViT architecture by replacing linear projections with PQCs, evaluates performance using standard metrics (Accuracy/Recall), and validates the quantum component using hardware fidelity measurements.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it demonstrates a concrete, end-to-end application of quantum machine learning (QML) to a major astrophysical data challenge, providing metrics for assessing near-term quantum advantage in data processing.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Architecture of the QViT identification model. Dynamic-spectrum images constructed from PSRFITS data are resized to 288 × 288 pixels, converted into tokens and passed to the hybrid transformer. Parameterized quantum circuits generate the query, key and value representations, while attention mixing and classification remain classical. The model returns an FRB-like proba- bility for each input segment.
Figure 2: Enhanced parameterized quantum circuit used for the Q/K/V projections and for real- device inference.

Figure 3: Performance comparison between QViT and classical ViT on the untouched test set. The horizontal axis denotes the number of trainable parameters in the Q/K/V projection module, computed as the total Q/K/V parameter count for each plotted configuration. (a) Classification accuracy. (b) Recall. Symbols indicate the mean over 10 independent seeds and error bars repre- sent one standard deviation. For the selected comparison used in the main text, QViT reaches an accuracy of 94.00 ± 0.48% and a recall of 98.30 ± 0.60%, compared with 93.83 ± 0.60% accuracy and 98.23 ± 0.22% recall for ViT.

Figure 4: Hellinger fidelity between simulated and real-device measurement distributions for the real-hardware validation samples. For each segment, the fidelity is averaged over its 204 Q/K/V cir- cuit evaluations. Across 82 hardware-validation segments, each circuit was executed with 20,000 shots, and the minimum segment-level mean fidelity is 0.8923.
